Photograph: Alamy View image in fullscreen The Guardian has seen internal DPD records detailing the costs of more than 3,000 temporary workers but they do not include any sick pay or pension. Photograph: Alamy Couriers/delivery industry DPD temporary workers may have missed out on sick pay and pensions, internal documents show Missing payments suggest employment laws may have been breached by recruitment agencies used by courier company Simon Goodley Sun 9 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Low-paid temporary workers at one of the UK’s top courier businesses have missed out on entitlements to sick pay and pension contributions, internal documents suggest. The payments – typically included in the “charge rate” that large brands pay recruitment companies to supply them with temporary workers – are missing from internal spreadsheets calculating the cost of employing thousands of transient staff working at DPD. This absence suggests workers have either not been paid their entitlements, were discouraged from taking days off when sick, or were removed from roles before pension contributions became due, experts said. Zoë Lagadec, principal at Mulberry’s employment law solicitors, said: “This raises questions if the workers are receiving statutory sick pay – as it doesn’t make sense that nobody gets ill – or if they are being moved on before 12 weeks service in order to avoid pension contributions.” Withholding sick pay or pension contributions when they come due would be a breach of employment law by recruitment agencies and seemingly contravenes industry guidance published by the Association of Labour Providers. The trade body’s charge rate guidance adds : “Supermarkets, brands and other labour users have a clear responsibility to ensure that labour providers throughout their supply chains are paid rates that fully reflect legal employment costs and compliance obligations. “Labour users that pay unrealistically low rates are knowingly or recklessly conniving in illegality as these rates can only be achieved through worker exploitation, tax evasion or both.” DPD promotes itself as “one of Europe’s leading parcel groups” and is wholly owned by France’s La Poste. It says its team exceeds 15,000 people , operating more than 10,000 vehicles from 84 locations and delivering more than 260m parcels a year. Its customers have included John Lewis , Marks & Spencer and Amazon . The Guardian has seen internal DPD records detailing the discrete costs of more than 3,000 temporary workers hired by the courier during the past two financial years. The documents include hourly pay rates, holiday pay, employer’s national insurance contributions and a margin for the temporary recruitment agency, but do not include any sick pay or pension. Industry experts questioned whether any temporary recruitment agency, which is technically the employer of the workers, could make any profit from DPD’s charge rates if it then paid the sick pay and pension entitlements to its thousands of staff. Sick pay is now a right on the first day’s absence, although before April it only became due after three days off. Pension contributions are paid by the employer after 12 weeks in the job. The Guardian outlined to DPD the records seen and what they appear to show. The company said: “Our commercial arrangements with our agencies allow them to fulfil their statutory obligations and are benchmarked against competitors in the industry.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Preview latest after newsletter promotion A spokesperson for the courier company added: “At DPD, we take our legal, regulatory and ethical responsibilities extremely seriously. As a client, engaging third-party employment agencies, DPD pays an agreed commercial charge rate to agency suppliers for providing temporary labour. “Under UK employment law, recruitment agencies act as the primary employers of these agency workers. Consequently, statutory obligations, including the administration and payment of Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) and auto-enrolment pension contributions, sit directly with the agency suppliers, rather than DPD as the end-user client. “Our contractual agreements require all agency partners to strictly follow all applicable employment legislation, including statutory pay and pension auto-enrolment requirements. We continuously review our procurement processes and supplier relationships to ensure our agency partners uphold the highest standards of compliance and fair treatment for all workers.” The discovery of the data comes as the temporary recruitment industry looks at how the government’s new Fair Work Agency, which came into existence on 7 April, will use its powers to enforce workers’ rights. The agency brings together much of the existing enforcement system into a single body, by combining the Gangmasters and Labour Abuse Authority, the Employment Agency Standards Inspectorate, HM Revenue and Customs’ national minimum wage enforcement unit and the Office of the Director of Labour Market Enforcement. https://www.odnako.org/secret-bases-for-.text: International “Secret bases for Russian superdrones, they may arrive in Warsaw”. Kiev raid, 9 dead By John 2026-08-23 Add the Gazzetta del Sud as a source Ten new secret bases from which to launch the most advanced models of its drones would have been built by Russia and already partly used to hammer Ukraine, which is increasingly short of air defenses. But from these sites the unmanned aircraft could also be launched “deep into NATO territory”, with Warsaw being within their range of action. This is stated by the Telegraph in an investigation based on the analysis of «leaked documents, satellite images» and data from the analysis company DroneSec. The 59 launch pads along the borders with Ukraine and Belarus The British newspaper claims to have identified “at least 59 launch pads” along the borders with Ukraine and Belarus from where the latest versions of the drones released from Russian factories could launch: jet aircraft “capable of reaching targets almost 620 miles away”. That is about a thousand kilometres. Always according to Telegraph seven of the ten bases were used by Moscow in the recent bombings of Kiev, but they could also be used against countries of the Atlantic Alliance in the event of a direct conflict. Satellite images would show a significant increase in supplies of high-tech drones. At least one of the bases would be able to store over a thousand aircraft ready for use. Nine dead in Russia in Ukrainian attacks Meanwhile, intense bombing by Ukrainian drones and missiles continues on various regions of Russia. After the seven deaths reported on Sunday, on Monday the Moscow authorities reported nine more killed: six in a missile attack in the Belgorod region, in the village of Koloskovo, one in the same oblast from a drone raid and one each, also killed by drones, in the Astrakhan and Bryansk regions. Moscow claims responsibility for the raids on Ukrainian ports Russian forces continue to concentrate in particular on bombing Ukrainian ports. Moscow’s Defense Ministry said a Tarantul-class motor torpedo boat and a ship unloading arms and ammunition for Ukrainian forces were hit in Odessa, on the Black Sea. Another cargo ship of this kind was bombed in the port of Mykolaiv, while in the port of Izmail, along the Danube on the border with Romania, “a docking terminal for the unloading of ships with cargoes of military use, hangars with Western military equipment, as well as warehouses for unmanned vessels” were targeted. Near Odessa, the Russian ministry adds, a logistics center of Nova Pochta, the largest private Ukrainian freight forwarder, was hit, whose sites have already been targeted several times in recent weeks. Kallas: «In autumn the widest list of sanctions since the beginning of the war» Meanwhile, EU High Representative Kaja Kallas, in an interview with the German newspaper Die Welt stated that «in the autumn the most extensive list of sanctions since the beginning of the war will be presented». “The pressure must be increased until Russia ends the war,” he added. Gallagher’s mission to Russia from 25 to 28 August The Secretary for Relations with States (the Foreign Minister) of the Vatican, Msgr. Paul Richard Gallagher, however, is expected for a mission to Russia from 25 to 28 August to evaluate whether it is possible to achieve “concrete results” in the diplomatic action of the Holy See. This is what the newspaper writes Nezavisimaia Gazeta . Gallagher himself and Cardinal Matteo Zuppi, the president of the Italian Episcopal Conference (CEI) who has twice carried out missions in Moscow, in 2023 and 2024, were in Kiev last month. And Zuppi himself is planning a new visit to Russia, probably in September. For Gallagher, he writes Nezavisimaia Gazeta it is important to ensure that Zuppi’s new mission does not result in a “diplomatic impasse” like the one that occurred in 2023, “when Russia flatly refused to discuss any political aspect of resolving the conflict with the papal envoy and the Vatican mission was reduced to dealing with humanitarian issues.” John John, founder of Odnako, combined his journalism degree with technical expertise to revolutionize global news consumption.
